entries.title: Ray-Ban Meta Audio Review: The Best Smart Glasses
entries.summary: No cameras? No problem. Ditching the surveillance baggage makes Meta’s audio-only frames surprisingly easy to live with.
entries.content:
I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.

“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”

The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.

This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.

It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.

It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)

It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)

entries.title: Garmin Vivoactive 5 and Forerunner 165 Are up to 30 Percent Off (2026)
entries.summary: I’ve tested almost every Garmin watch—these entry-level favorites are steeply discounted right now.
entries.content:
Garmin watches are some of the best fitness trackers you can get, but they aren't exactly cheap—some cost over $1,000. Thankfully, with some patience and brand know-how, you can actually get a great Garmin watch for less than $200. Right now, some of my favorite entry-level models, including the Garmin Vivoactive 5 and Garmin Forerunner 165, are over 20 percent off. If you've been thinking about trying out Garmin, now is a good time to buy.

For more wearable recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Garmin Watches, Best Smartwatches, Best Smart Rings, and Best Sleep Trackers.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Garmin Vivoactive 5 for $198 ($102 Off)

The Vivoactive 5 is a great first Garmin watch, and it's 34 percent off right now. It's an older model (it launched in 2023), but you still have many of the brand's best fitness and health features available, including in-depth fitness metrics, Body Battery (basically your energy score throughout the day), sleep coaching, and stress tracking. It's also small, lightweight, and a little sleeker than some of the brand's more outdoor-centric watches.

Garmin Forerunner 165 for $197 ($53 Off)

The Forerunner 165 is probably the best value per dollar for any runner looking to start using a Garmin watch. It has a bright, colorful touchscreen and Garmin's classic five-button control layout—three buttons on the left side of the watch, two on the right. The ample buttons make it easy to control this watch, even when I'm running outside with gloves on. It has Garmin's typical long battery life: up to 11 days. And it has many of Garmin's detailed running and training metrics, including detailed running info, Garmin training plans, daily suggested workouts, and training effect (based on aerobic and anaerobic load).

Garmin Venu 3 for $299 ($151 Off)

This is a sneaky-good deal on an older Garmin watch from 2023. Think of the Garmin Venu like if the Vivoactive had a major glow-up. The Venu 3 has a stainless steel bezel that makes the whole watch look a little more classy, plus built-in speakers and microphones, so you can take a call from your wrist. Despite its age, it has Garmin's latest Elevate 5 heart rate sensor built in, meaning more accurate data and an ECG sensor.
